items.title: Verifiable Incentives: Identity-Bound Contracts and Collusion-Proof Delegation for Agent Commerce
items.abstract: Abstract Personal agents are entering commerce. Industry protocols now let an agent prove, cryptographically, whom it represents and what it may do, while agent wallets give it a real budget, a payment trail, and one-time merchant credentials. These are usually read as security features. We argue they are something more: the missing infrastructure for incentive contracts. When identity, authority, budget, and payment are verifiable, the principal can contract on them-and the agent's incentives change. We formalize verifiable delegation, model a three-party market of user, agent, and merchant, and derive three results: (i) verifiable identity lowers the bonus and tenure needed to sustain effort; (ii) auditable payments bound merchant collusion, with collusion becoming unprofitable as audit probability rises; and (iii) a posted honesty stake substitutes for monitoring, with the required stake decreasing in audit quality and penalty credibility. We also show how alignment dilutes along nested delegation chains unless contracts are passed through. We instantiate the framework in PAIR-Commerce, an architecture with a verifiable identity layer, wallet ledger, sponsorship registry, collusion monitor, and stake manager, and introduce AgentCommerce-Bench, 60 rule-scored purchasing tasks with five delegation regimes. In three instruction-following studies-600 single-shot runs, an 800-round payment sandbox, and a 1,200-run high-pressure replication-agents rarely collude even when hidden sponsorship is available; a semi-field task set built from real merchant catalogs shows the same pattern. But when the same models are instructed to maximize their own earnings, collusion jumps to 48.3% without audit and falls to 33-40% with audit and penalties (8-15 percentage points lower; 95% CI excludes zero for two of three models); in a second, 800-round economic sandbox, it falls from 29.5% without audit to 3-4% with audit and penalties, and the agent's balance turns negative once the stake is posted. The mechanism binds exactly when the agent's objective makes it bind. We release the benchmark, prompts, code, and all result files.

ChainIT Transaction Truth: Stablecoins, Web3 Wallets, and Multi-Rail Commerce. A Zero-Trust Control Plane for Verified Identity, Organizational Authority, Runtime Compliance, Secure Wallet Execution, and Immutable Settlement Evidence
items.abstract: Stablecoins can move value continuously across programmable networks, and Web3 wallets can authorize those transfers with cryptographic signatures, but neither capability, standing alone, establishes a complete commercial transaction. A blockchain may prove that a transaction satisfied protocol rules, and a wallet may prove that sufficient signing authority existed; neither proves who initiated the transaction, for which legal entity, under what current authority, against which current compliance evidence, on what exact instruction, or with what settlement and accounting outcome. We describe the ChainIT Transaction Truth Architecture, a zero-trust control, execution, and evidence architecture that places verified individual and organizational identity, the organizational authority record and authority policy of the ChainIT Authority Protocol, transaction-specific runtime compliance decisions, exact-digest approval, atomic capacity reservation, and a single-use Execution Authorization Credential in front of wallet execution, and that records settlement, reconciliation, and lifecycle evidence after the transaction. The architecture separates five boundaries: control of a key is not identity, identity is not organizational authority, authority is not compliance, compliance is not execution authority, and network confirmation is not complete commercial settlement. We describe wallet and custody profiles, including a multi-party computation (MPC) profile in which custody security is kept independent of business authority, stablecoin and Web3 evidence domains, layered finality, the U.S. stablecoin regulatory context as of September 2026, and a phased deployment in which pilot success requires that the control invariants hold under attack and failure.

Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI): A Federated Identity, Trust, Attestation, and Accountability Architecture for Cross-Organization Autonomous AI Agents
items.abstract: AI agents increasingly collaborate across organizational boundaries, invoking tools and interacting with agents operated by independent entities. Although existing agent frameworks support planning and coordination, they lack a common mechanism for verifying cross-organizational agent identity, execution integrity, and authorization. We propose the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent security architecture built on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), and remote attestation. ATI establishes federated trust through peer organizational certificate authorities (AgentCAs), eliminating the need for a shared root authority. Before executing requests, ATI validates agent certificates, verifies approved model, tool, and system-prompt configurations, and enforces authorization through three policy checks. We implement ATI as an external security enforcement layer that integrates with existing agent frameworks without modifying their underlying models. We evaluate ATI in a simulated federation of eight organizations using six agent frameworks, each deploying a five-agent team. Security experiments involve two organizations and assess 14 attack scenarios and six benign tasks across five agent models, using five attack variations and three repetitions per variation. A panel of judge models evaluates the experimental outcomes. With all enforcement mechanisms enabled, attack containment increases from 43% to 84% (40% to 80% for the 11 attack scenarios evaluated consistently across all configurations), while enforcement introduces approximately 174 microseconds of overhead per request. ATI is released as an open-source, framework-independent package that uses IETF WIMSE workload token formats for identity and request verification and Entity Attestation Tokens for model, tool, and system-prompt integrity verification.

Discovering Agentic AI: Discovery, Preservation, and Proof in AI and Agentic Systems
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems evolve beyond conversational interfaces into multi-step workflows capable of retrieving information, maintaining state, invoking tools, delegating tasks, and acting across external systems, electronic discovery faces increasingly complex evidentiary questions. A user-facing transcript or current system configuration may not establish what information an AI system received, what instructions and controls governed its behavior, what actions it was authorized to perform, or what consequences resulted from a disputed historical execution.This white paper examines the application of United States federal civil discovery and evidence law to AI and agentic systems. Drawing on emerging judicial decisions and established electronic discovery principles, it analyzes relevance, proportionality, preservation, possession, custody or control, privilege, production, authentication, and expert proof. It identifies potential evidentiary sources across system and developer instructions, model configurations, retrieval-augmented generation, tool and API schemas, Model Context Protocol (MCP) interactions, agent memory, orchestration, delegated authority, execution traces, configuration histories, and downstream business records.The paper advances reconstructable execution state as a proposition-centered analytical framework for identifying the minimum historically accurate evidence necessary to evaluate a disputed AI execution. It distinguishes technical capability from authorization, attempted actions from completed effects, present-day configurations from historical conditions, and contemporaneous records from inference or later reconstruction.Integrating recent AI-related discovery developments with practical preservation, collection, and evidentiary methods, the paper proposes an execution-centered approach to identifying relevant sources, reconstructing historical system behavior, and evaluating evidentiary reliability. Its central argument is that agentic AI does not require a separate discovery regime, but rather a more rigorous application of existing law to dynamic, distributed, and version-dependent evidence.

Bajillion: Cryptographic Clearing for Micropayments
items.abstract: Much of the web is funded by advertising, a model that erodes as humans delegate browsing to AI agents acting on their behalf. A natural replacement is for agents to pay for what they consume, often a fraction of a cent per request. At the scale of web traffic, this could mean tens or even hundreds of millions of payments per second. We present Bajillion, a clearing protocol for scalable micropayments. A sender signs a payment request, and an untrusted operator answers with a preconfirmation, which promises the receiver that it will be paid. Periodically, the operator closes an epoch by posting only the net effect of its payments on chain. Bajillion guarantees that a malicious operator can only omit payments -- it can never debit a sender beyond what it signed, nor misdirect a transfer. Posted balances are therefore finalized immediately and can be withdrawn. By design, senders never have to raise disputes, making it suitable for ephemeral AI agents. A receiver that is shortchanged can prove that a close omitted a preconfirmed payment, which halts the protocol and lets every user exit with its finalized balance. Requests from different senders can be processed independently, allowing the operator to parallelize up to the number of senders. We capture these guarantees in an ideal functionality for accountable clearing and prove that Bajillion realizes it.

Agent-ZTA: A chain-Aware Zero Trust Model for Bidirectional Security-State Propagation and Runtime Containment in Multi-Agent Delegation
items.abstract: Multi-agent systems increasingly delegate tasks and permissions across chains of autonomous agents that invoke protected tools. Although agent identities and delegated credentials may remain valid throughout a workflow, the security condition of any agent along the chain can deteriorate during runtime execution-either through upstream compromise or downstream ingestion of untrusted inputs. Authorization models based solely on the immediate caller and its static delegated scope fail to account for these mid-execution state changes. This paper develops Agent-ZTA, a chain-aware Zero Trust authorization and containment model that links runtime security-state changes across multi-agent delegation graphs. The model distinguishes an agent's path-specific delegated authority bound from the effective permissions currently exercisable under trusted policy. It defines an architecture featuring independently enforced policy decisions, authenticated delegation provenance, a dynamic chain-state view, and explicit fail-safe handling of missing or stale authorization signals. Furthermore, Agent-ZTA defines bidirectional security state propagation, allowing downstream security events to affect relevant upstream workflow states, and specifies adaptive branch-scoped containment through restricted permissions and a sandbox ("jail") execution mode where an isolation boundary is available. The deterministic decision procedure, five stated security properties, and worked authorization traces show how accepted security-state changes constrain affected operations while preserving original delegation bounds and separating unrelated workflow branches under the defined policies. Finally, the paper states its trust assumptions and the exact scope of its security properties.

Cortex-FL: Agent-Mediated Collaboration for Federated Learning
items.abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables independent data owners to train models collaboratively without centralizing raw data. However, identifying collaborators, preparing training tasks, and coordinating execution and incentives hinder its practical adoption by organizations without specialized expertise. We present Cortex-FL, an agent-native FL system that enables users to express learning objectives in natural language and delegate the collaboration required to train a model. Agents translate these objectives into shared tasks, discover collaborators, and negotiate participation agreements, connecting collaboration formation with distributed training and incentive management. The architecture separates agent coordination from local execution authority, allowing owners to delegate coordination while retaining control over their data, computation, and financial commitments. We demonstrate the complete workflow on a four-node deployment, in which a model requested in natural language proceeds through collaboration formation, contract-governed training, verified model delivery, and x402 settlement on a blockchain testnet.

items.title: China's Local Government Debt, Strategic Competition, and Bitcoin Demand: A Conditional Transmission Framework
items.abstract: How might the resolution of China's local-government debt affect strategic competition and Bitcoin demand? This paper develops a conditional framework connecting debt accounting, bank balance-sheet adjustment, public spending priorities, and constrained portfolio substitution. A debt swap can increase recognized government debt without increasing consolidated principal, while its effect on credit capacity depends on capital relief, loss recognition, and recapitalization. A protected strategic-spending floor can preserve current effort while shifting adjustment toward civilian productive services. In the asset block, stronger relative preference for Bitcoin does not ensure greater effective demand: access constraints and global funding conditions can reverse the sign. We derive a finite-shock threshold and deterministic sign bounds, and distinguish Bitcoin demand from demand for dollar stablecoins. Reproducible numerical illustrations and channel-removal exercises show that opposite outcomes are compatible with the same assumed fiscal stress. The analysis uses dated primary sources to establish institutional context, but estimates neither a debt-to-Bitcoin causal coefficient nor a price-impact scale. Its contribution is a compact set of conditions and measurement distinctions for evaluating transmission claims, rather than an unconditional price forecast or an inference about conflict probabilities.

items.title: Secure and Governed Multi-Agent AI Architectures Using Identity-Aware Authorization and Fine-Grained Access Control
items.venue: International Journal of Engineering & Extended Technologies Research
items.abstract: The growing adoption of multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) systems within enterprise environments has introduced new challenges in securing autonomous interactions, controlling access to sensitive resources, and maintaining governance across distributed computational workflows. Unlike conventional AI applications, multi-agent architectures involve multiple autonomous entities that independently interpret tasks, exchange contextual information, invoke external tools, and coordinate decisions across heterogeneous enterprise systems. These capabilities introduce complex security risks associated with unauthorized resource access, excessive agent privileges, identity impersonation, unintended information disclosure, and insufficient accountability for machine-generated actions. Traditional role-based authorization models and perimeter-oriented security mechanisms are often inadequate for managing the dynamic relationships and contextual dependencies inherent in autonomous agent ecosystems. This article presents a generalized architectural framework for designing secure and governed multi-agent AI systems through identity-aware authorization, fine-grained access control, and policy-driven governance mechanisms. The proposed approach integrates workload identity management, attribute-based access control, policy-based authorization, least-privilege enforcement, and continuous trust evaluation to establish verifiable security boundaries between agents, tools, data resources, and enterprise services. Particular emphasis is placed on securing agent-to-agent communication, enforcing context-sensitive permissions during tool execution, managing delegated authority, and establishing auditable decision pathways across distributed workflows. The architecture further incorporates centralized policy decision capabilities, distributed enforcement mechanisms, cryptographic identity verification, and continuous monitoring to support scalable governance without unnecessarily restricting agent autonomy. The study examines architectural components, authorization workflows, operational security considerations, and evaluation criteria for implementing trustworthy multi-agent platforms. By combining identity-centric security principles with adaptive authorization and governance controls, the proposed framework provides a foundation for developing enterprise AI ecosystems that balance autonomous execution, operational scalability, regulatory accountability, and protection of organizational information assets.

items.title: Agentic Commerce and the Economics of Machine-to-Machine Payments
items.abstract: We define agentic commerce as the delegation of commercial decisions and payments to artificial intelligence (AI) and provide statistics on prices and services using data from Coinbase’s x402 Protocol and Tempo & Stripe’s Machine Payments Protocol. Despite more than 234 million recorded transactions, activity across these protocols consists largely of pay-per-use micropayments for digital resources, while observed x402 usage is concentrated among a small number of services, many of which report few paying accounts. Agentic commerce can reduce search and transaction costs, but it also creates governance and accountability problems when AI agents make persistent errors, interact strategically, or are manipulated, potentially generating negative distributional and welfare effects. This review also discusses regulatory approaches and identifies priorities for AI governance and future research.

A transaction control layer for governed agentic commerce: reference architecture implementation and controlled evaluation
items.venue: Journal of Computer Science and Technology Studies
items.abstract: A weak answer from a shopping assistant may inconvenience a customer. A weak action from a commerce agent can move money, reserve inventory, change a delivery commitment, or issue a refund. Once an agent can create those effects, the central question is no longer whether its response sounds correct. The question is whether the action is still authorized and commercially valid when the enterprise system commits it. This study introduces a Transaction Control Layer (TCL) that separates an agent's proposal from permission to execute. TCL binds each approved action to grounded intent, delegated authority, current authoritative state, a short validity period, and a stable idempotency key. It then records and reconciles the resulting side effects. We formalize commit validity across five dimensions and define five operational decisions: allow, modify, hold, deny, and escalate. The design is examined with CAV-Bench v1.0.0, an Apache-2.0 reference artifact containing 40 synthetic scenarios and five deterministic architecture profiles. The direct profile reaches an outcome success rate of 0.925, yet only 0.250 of its runs are commit-valid. Adding policy checks, commit-time guards, reconciliation, and lifecycle recovery raises commit-valid success to 0.500, 0.750, 0.875, and 1.000. These values show that the benchmark responds to the controls it was designed to test. They do not estimate real model failure rates or establish production effectiveness. An external replication protocol is therefore included as the next step toward independent validation.

items.title: AI shopping agents and the reallocation of consumer attention: seller visibility and platform access in agentic commerce
items.venue: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
items.abstract: Purpose This study develops a theoretical model of how AI shopping agents reallocate shopping activity, reshape seller visibility and alter platform control in digital commerce. Consumer attention is defined as the allocation of shopping episodes across channels, distinct from visual or cognitive attention. Design/methodology/approach A two-seller platform model compares platform-mediated and AI-agent-mediated shopping. The platform chooses agent access and ranking bias; sellers choose price, platform-facing visibility and agent-facing adaptation. Heterogeneous AI-use costs make channel use endogenous, while a fixed implementation cost creates an adaptation threshold. Extensions separate information access from transaction execution and test the robustness of the analytical regimes numerically. Findings Agent access is profitable when transaction and AI-channel gains outweigh lost ranking monetization and governance costs, and information access may remain open while transaction execution is restricted. Sellers activate agent-facing adaptation only when its incremental return covers implementation cost. AI-mediated shopping lowers prices when comparison pressure dominates verified differentiation. Ranking mismatch can turn the two visibility investments from complements into competing activities, and privately optimal openness can fall outside the welfare-improving interval. Originality/value Four features distinguish AI shopping agents from platform recommenders and comparison sites: delegated choice authority, cross-platform scope, multi-stage task execution and an independently governed ranking layer. The framework links these features to layered platform access, endogenous AI-channel use, distinct visibility investments, implementation costs, verifiable trust signals and divergence between private and social incentives in agentic commerce.

Enterprise Agent Identity Governance Framework (EAIGF): A Policy-Mediated Identity and Access Governance Model for Autonomous Digital Workforce Systems
items.venue: International Journal of Cyber Threat Intelligence and Secure Networking
items.abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are evolving from passive decision-support tools into autonomous digital workers capable of planning, reasoning, invoking tools, accessing enterprise resources, and executing business actions with varying degrees of autonomy. While enterprises maintain mature governance models for human identities, service accounts, and application identities, existing Identity and Access Management (IAM) frameworks do not adequately address the governance challenges introduced by autonomous agents. Unlike conventional applications, agents dynamically determine execution paths, invoke reusable skills, delegate tasks to peer agents, and perform privileged actions across enterprise systems. These characteristics define a new class of enterprise identity that requires dedicated governance, authorization, and accountability controls. This paper proposes the Enterprise Agent Identity Governance Framework (EAIGF), which treats autonomous agents as first-class enterprise identities subject to lifecycle management, quantitative trust classification, privileged access governance, and end-to-end accountability. The framework's principal constructs form an identity layer comprising the Agent Identity Registry (AIR), the Agent Provisioning Certificate, Agent Trust Tiering driven by an explicit Agent Identity Risk Score (AIRS) formula, Agent Privileged Access Management (Agent-PAM), and a Delegated Trust Chain with Agent Identity Lineage for multi-agent accountability. These constructs are enforced through a policy-mediated runtime boundary that performs capability projection and risk-adaptive authorization. A reference implementation realizing the registry, the AIRS formula, capability projection, and risk-adaptive authorization correctly enforced all ten governance scenarios in the evaluation with zero false-permits on disallowed capabilities and a mean authorization overhead of approximately 0.015 ms per request. A larger randomized evaluation over 600 authorization requests across 80 agents and 25 reusable skills reproduced this result and, against a naive whole-skill authorization baseline, reduced the exposed capability surface by 66.7 percent while blocking every attempted privilege escalation through delegation. A synthetic financial-services walkthrough demonstrates how Identity Governance and Administration (IGA), Privileged Access Management (PAM), and Zero Trust principles extend to agentic environments. EAIGF provides a practical blueprint for governing autonomous agents at scale while preserving least privilege, accountability, and operational resilience.

items.title: Resource Locks and Fast Unlock for Shared Balances in Certificate-Based Payment Systems
items.abstract: Certificate-based payment systems such as FastPay settle a payment with one round of signatures from a quorum of validators and avoid global ordering. The client collects the signatures, and validators never talk to each other. We observe that this client-driven design is complete only as long as no lock is ever undone. Each account has a single writer, a conflict can only come from that writer's own misbehavior, and the account stays locked as the penalty. Stablecoin payments routinely need balances that several accounts debit: treasuries, merchant pools, allowances and subscriptions. There, honest accounts race, locks must be undone, and a quorum certificate held privately by a client can be silently overridden. We prove that no unlock rule is safe in this setting unless certificate formation is visible to validators. We present a hybrid protocol. Personal accounts keep the client-driven FastPay path unchanged. A shared resource is a balance with its own version number and a set of authorized accounts. Transactions on shared resources are submitted to any validator and certified by a two-phase broadcast, ECHO then READY. The admission check requires both the sender's nonce and the resource's nonce to be free. Without contention, this path needs no consensus. When concurrent debits split the votes in any proportion, validators detect the split themselves, freeze the affected resource version, and resolve it with one agreement instance scoped to that version. Losing transactions return their sender nonce. We prove consistency, no overdraft, validity, finality and liveness. The protocol composes with the PDCC reconfiguration protocol.

items.title: Developing Consumer Trust in Sustainable Agentic Commerce: Conditional Signals, Auditable Governance, and Justified Non-Purchase Advice
items.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) changes digital retail from consumer-led search to delegated decision making, increasing both the potential value and the agency risks of recommendation. This conceptual article asks the following: Under what architectural and governance conditions can an autonomous shopping agent earn calibrated consumer trust while supporting economically and environmentally appropriate consumption decisions? Using a purposive, multidisciplinary synthesis of signaling theory, principal–agent theory, the ability–benevolence–integrity model of trust, trustworthy AI, recommender system governance, and sustainable consumption research, we develop a process model linking four architectural features to consumer perceptions, delegation, reliance, and decision outcomes. The features are scoped provenance verification, disclosed and audited commercial incentives, faithful contrastive explanations, and active evaluation of retention, repair, refurbishment, and purchase. We argue that justified non-purchase advice can function as a credible signal of consumer alignment only when the operator is the signal sender, the advice creates observable opportunity or accountability costs, and compensation and audit arrangements make imitation more costly for a misaligned operator. The framework distinguishes perceived trustworthiness from overall trust, willingness to delegate, actual reliance, recommendation appropriateness, and lifecycle sustainability. A five-layer architecture, a worked decision example, and four testable propositions specify how missing data, conflicting preferences, uncertainty, authorization, privacy, and accountability should be handled. This article treats the applications as illustrations rather than empirical cases and concludes with limitations and an empirical research agenda focused on calibrated—not merely increased—trust.

I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
items.abstract: Human oversight is a pillar of AI safety. It is often exercised by a human in the loop (HITL) who approves critical actions taken by an AI agent. AI agents' increasing ability to bypass guardrails, though, raises the question of how to enforce HITL robustly. We introduce the concept of inalienable human-in-the-loop (I-HITL). An I-HITL protocol ensures that an agent can initiate an action only with explicit human approval, even when the human interacts with a system (e.g., a local agentic harness) compromised by the agent. A strong I-HITL protocol additionally ensures such approval even when an adversarial human attempts to delegate approvals to an agent. To motivate I-HITL, we report on experiments with a popular agentic wallet platform in which raising an agent's spending cap requires HITL approval via emailed one-time passcodes (OTPs). Given access to the user's email and a task blocked by the cap, we find that ten different frontier models will often autonomously raise the cap, harvesting OTPs to bypass a HITL guardrail and surfacing other vulnerabilities. We formally define I-HITL using the concept of communication topologies and prove necessary and sufficient conditions for its realization. We show that an I-HITL protocol requires a trusted entity - a trusted computing device (or equivalent) - and characterize which such devices can and cannot realize an I-HITL protocol. We present a prototype I-HITL system called Countersign that can plug into and strengthen existing HITL systems using off-the-shelf consumer mobile devices.

items.title: Breaking the Peg, or Not: The Limited Power of Oracle Manipulation Against Early Stablecoin Depeg Prediction
items.abstract: A common worry about depeg predictors is that an adversary who manipulates oracle prices can blind them. We test it on a new multi-source corpus of twelve historical stress episodes across nine assets and three chains. Under retrospective leave-one-event-out testing, the reconstructed models span 0.558–0.772 ROC-AUC, with our reference predictor at 0.762; the source papers report different metrics and tasks that are not directly comparable. Manipulable price features hurt out-of-event generalization: on the seven-episode live-feed subgroup, retained features reach 0.75 AUC versus 0.72 for the full model, directional, not significant at seven events. We define the Oracle Manipulation Index (OMI), prove that shifting the aggregate by δ while one honest feed survives forces the unnormalized cross-feed price range to be at least δ/L for L-Lipschitz aggregators, and measure on a Foundry mainnet fork (Curve 3pool, block 25,238,878) that a 0.1% move requires about USD 50 M in deployed capital. Excluding individually affordable channels gives a sufficient input-invariance rule under fixed channel costs; the robust subset matches clean accuracy and degrades less under tested synthetic attacks in point estimate (directional, not significant at seven events). OMI’s empirical lift is modest and regime-dependent (pooled 0.0037, not significant; it helps off-chain and multi-venue settings, not single-venue on-chain ones), and precision is low (about 33 false-positive windows per true-positive window at 10% recall). Within this early-warning setting, oracle manipulation is a weak evasion vector because the tested subset is empirically less sensitive to the evaluated perturbations.

items.title: FlockWorld: Toward Population-Scale Multi-Agent Video World Models through Artificial Life Simulation
items.abstract: Most action-conditioned video world models remain limited to a single player, while existing multiplayer models support only small, fixed groups of agents. We introduce FlockWorld, an artificial-life environment built on Reynolds's Boids algorithm for studying population-scale multi-agent video world models. Specifically, FlockWorld renders synchronized egocentric crops, assigns distinct colors to preserve camera-agent identity across views, exposes rule-derived accelerations as actions, and lets the number of camera agents be configured independently of the size of the surrounding population. We further introduce FlockDiT, an action-conditioned latent diffusion transformer trained with flow matching on FlockWorld data to jointly generate synchronized egocentric videos for multiple agents. Our results suggest that joint generation benefits agent detection at density-matched settings and that diffusion forcing improves rollout fidelity. Together, FlockWorld and FlockDiT provide a controlled testbed for multi-agent video generation.

items.title: Algernon – A B2B compliance and security oracle for AI agents on Base via x402
Evervault Browser Tokens: Agentic payments on any website
Markets of Minds: A 51-Billion-State Economy of Intelligence
items.abstract: When intelligence is shared, reasoning becomes a constrained allocation problem. In a population of agents with limited access to expert models, an intervention can benefit its recipient yet still be a poor use of shared capacity if another feasible intervention has greater expected value. Assistance must therefore be evaluated through both its marginal benefit and the opportunity cost induced by budgets, access, scarcity, and service capacity. To this end, we introduce Markets of Minds, a framework for allocating expert reasoning across agents before expert outputs are observed. For each feasible agent-service pair, the framework estimates the expected gain from assistance relative to the agent's default continuation, explicitly separating repair benefit from regression risk, and jointly clears assistance contracts under shared resource constraints. We then study this problem in a dependency-aware agent economy with 51.2 billion addressable persona-market states spanning capabilities, cognitive budgets, provider access, scarcity, and network roles. These dependencies couple allocation feasibility across agents rather than the outcome of a fixed contract. Empirically, in a matched replay of 240 cases under a common 30% assistance quota, the frozen allocator reaches 85.42% task-level persona adherence versus 73.86% for equal-capacity random allocation, a gain of 11.56 percentage points. The results show that assistance value is heterogeneous and can be negative, and that scarcity changes which interventions are worth purchasing. Together, these findings motivate a population-level view of intelligence where the value of assistance depends not only on what it can achieve, but also on which alternative uses of scarce cognitive capacity it displaces.

items.abstract: The OCC, as part of its continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burden, invites comment on a new information collection, as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA). items.title: Stablecoin Liquidity and U.S. Monetary Policy Transmission
Price insurance or cash-flow insurance? Energy subsidies and targeted transfers in a heterogeneous-agent economy
items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines whether generalized energy subsidies or targeted cash transfers provide more effective stabilization in an economy with heterogeneous households and segmented labor markets. We develop a small-open-economy Heterogeneous-Agent New Keynesian (HANK-DSGE) model calibrated to Morocco, incorporating heterogeneity in marginal propensities to consume (MPCs), formal–informal–agricultural labor-market segmentation, imported energy, remittances, and exchange-rate management. An agricultural productivity experiment identifies sectoral wage adjustment as an important mechanism transmitting shocks through household labor income. The central policy experiment compares generalized energy subsidies with subsidy removal and a budget-neutral reallocation of the same state-contingent fiscal outlay toward targeted transfers. Targeted transfers direct 81.8% of expenditure toward high-MPC households, compared with 10.6% of the dividend-mediated incidence of subsidies. Following an oil-price shock, redirecting subsidy expenditure toward targeted transfers reduces the impact consumption loss from 1.05% to 0.51% and the welfare loss from 0.40% to 0.22%, while increasing short-run inflation pass-through. The results identify a policy frontier between price insurance and cash-flow insurance and show that MPC-weighted fiscal incidence is central to the stabilization effects of alternative fiscal instruments. JEL Classification: E21; E62; H22; H23; Q43

items.title: SaaS in the Agent Economy: Why AI Just Changed Bootstrapped SaaS Forever [video]
Proof-Carrying Contracts: Commitments AI Agents Cannot Break
items.abstract: AI agents increasingly act on behalf of people or other agents, purchasing services, exchanging information and delegating work. What an agent must respect is written in instructions, policies or agreements, but text alone cannot make it comply. It may make mistakes, be redirected by what it reads, or pursue different interests. For an economy of such agents to function, parties need agreements they can rely on without inspecting or trusting one another's agents. We introduce Proof-Carrying Contracts (PC2), a framework for making agreed constraints enforceable throughout an agent's interactions with a system. Before a requested operation can run, the agent must supply a machine-checkable proof that it preserves the agreed constraints in every case allowed by its model. An execution system called the Airlock checks the proof and controls access to the operation. The parties specify the conditions to preserve, while the agent supplies the reasoning needed to justify its decisions and remains free to adapt its strategy. This avoids having to design a separate permission policy and prove that every decision it permits is safe. We prove that the constraints hold at every instant during execution, even for an adversarial agent, and identify when this implies safety in the world. Reusable capability modules provide tools and guarantees from which contracts can be constructed. PC2 provides a foundation for an agent economy whose agreements protect both those delegating work and those carrying it out.

items.title: Provable Authority: A Protocol for Verifiable Authority Resolution and Control Across Human, Organizational, and Agentic Transactions
items.abstract: Payment systems authenticate users, devices, accounts, and cryptographic credentials, but a relying party, such as a counterparty, payment rail, marketplace, or autonomous agent runtime, generally cannot obtain compact, independently verifiable evidence that the party presenting one exact transaction holds current organizational authority to execute it under the applicable evidence, policy, budget, and approval state. Agentic commerce makes this gap operationally urgent: a software agent can produce a valid signature while acting outside its delegated purpose, after its sponsor's authority has changed, or on transaction details that differ from those a human approved. We describe the ChainIT Authority Protocol, a subject-neutral and rail-neutral pre-execution authority and evidence control plane. The protocol separates durable identity, a versioned organizational authority record (the Authority Resolution Pactvera), sourced evidence assertions, deterministic reason-coded policy predicates, and organization-configured dispositions; binds each decision and human approval to a canonical transaction digest; reserves capacity atomically so that limits hold under concurrency; and authorizes commit only through a single-use, sender-constrained Execution Authorization Credential consumed at the rail adapter, with append-only lifecycle evidence sealed after the terminal outcome. An Agent Subject Profile adds the workload registration, attested key hierarchy, and sovereignty boundary required when the acting subject is an AI agent, without introducing a separate authority concept. We specify the commit-time execution predicate and bounded-freshness status rules, give enforcement profiles for fiat (ACH, wire, card, instant payment) and stablecoin rails, and state residual risks and non-goals.

items.title: From authorization to defensibility: enterprise stablecoin compliance readiness after the GENIUS Act
items.venue: Journal of Financial Regulation and Compliance
items.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine how organizational actors translate statutory authorization of payment stablecoins into judgments of compliance readiness for enterprise use. Design/methodology/approach The study uses 23 short stimulus-based interviews conducted after the U.S. GENIUS Act: 22 organizational informants and one finance-domain informant. Abductive thematic analysis combined evidence weighting, negative cases and stimulus and timing sensitivity checks. Findings Authorization increased discussability but not defensibility. Readiness required workflow value, an assurance bundle, operational absorbability, gatekeeper movement and a credible regulatory signal. Some participants instead regarded stablecoins as redundant because existing rails already met their needs; where value existed, unresolved custody, controls, systems and counterparty acceptance delayed use. Research limitations/implications The data capture first-pass, role-informed judgments in a short, network-recruited design; they do not observe deliberation or implementation. The construct is a sensitizing framework, not a tested causal model. Practical implications The framework provides a diagnostic: identify the payment pain, document assurance, test operational fit and locate the blocking gatekeeper. Social implications Public-payer, healthcare and nonprofit cases show that modernization can affect access, confidentiality, stewardship and familiar payment options. Originality/value The paper develops regulatory-compliance readiness lag: the perceived interval between legal authorization and organizationally defensible payment use.

items.title: Cryptographically Secure Agent-to-Agent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems
items.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) comprise AI agents that collaborate or compete to perform complex, distributed tasks. Their dynamic interactions create opportunities for threat actors to target and impersonate other agents, intercept messages, inject malicious prompts, and exfiltrate sensitive data while simultaneously complicating the detection of anomalous behavior through conventional monitoring. This paper surveys threats and cryptographic challenges in agent-to-agent communication and presents a zero-trust architecture integrating identity, transport security, message integrity, and monitoring. The architecture establishes agent identities via decentralized identifiers and task-scoped verifiable credentials backed by a permissioned ledger, enforcing least-privilege authorization. For transport security, it provides mutually authenticated, crypto-agile TLS with hybrid post-quantum key establishment, and evaluates KEMTLS with pre-distributed public keys to reduce handshake overhead. Signed CBOR envelopes preserve payload integrity across multi-hop exchanges, while zero-knowledge proofs verify declared task constraints without exposing underlying inputs. Context-aware monitoring of inter-agent messages, tool activity, and execution telemetry informs the setting of risk-based trust thresholds and supports the detection of behavioral anomalies. Together, these mechanisms provide an integrated framework for securing and auditing agent communication, with implications for other agentic protocols and prospective 6G semantic communication.

items.title: Approve What, Exactly? Effect Binding and Trusted Rendering for Agent Step-Up Authorization
items.abstract: AI agents now pause for approval before they send money, delete files or email outsiders, and that approval is usually treated as a second factor. We argue it is one only when compromising the agent cannot produce it and when it names exactly what it approves, and we test both conditions. We define twelve attacks on the approval path, including decoy recipients, amount cancellation, card padding, label spoofing, enrollment squatting and threshold splitting, and run them against the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), the Microsoft action-bound approval design and Model Context Protocol (MCP) elicitation. An audit of ten agent runtimes finds no third-party verifiable approval record, no flood limits where measurable, and post-approval argument changes in four of eight runtimes with measurable binding. As a reference defense we build ASU (Agent Step-Up), a gateway that renders the approval card from a canonical effect descriptor, has a passkey on the phone of the user sign its digest, and executes only the stored call. Tamarin proves its binding, single-use and key-level non-repudiation properties under three stated hypotheses (53 lemmas). Across 27,108 scripted trials and 609 AgentDojo attack pairs, ASU stops substitution, replay and grant stretching, and the trusted card cuts forged-narration attack success from 0.54 to 0.03. With 15 current language models as automated approvers, the trusted card raises the attack catch rate from 0.30 to 0.98, at the cost of refusing 16 percent of harmless near misses, mostly due to a placeholder artifact in our stimuli. A second device adds nothing measurable over a trusted on-host confirmation in these experiments, flooding still succeeds 0.45 to 0.60 of the time against a modeled approver, and approval cannot stop effects that policy already allows. Code, data and proofs: https://github.com/Sports-Vision-Inc/agent-step-up

items.title: Chính sách quản lý Agent Economy trong thời đại số: bài học kinh nghiệm cho việt nam Policy Frameworks for Governing the Agent Economy in the Digital Age: Lessons for Vietnam
items.venue: Tạp chí Khoa học và Công nghệ Trường Đại học Công nghệ Đông Á
items.abstract: The rapid emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is ushering in a new “Agent Economy” (AE), in which autonomous AI agents act on behalf of humans to perform complex tasks. While the Agent Economy promises substantial gains in productivity and innovation, it simultaneously presents profound governance challenges related to data privacy, security, ethics, and job displacement. A pressing concern is how humans can effectively oversee and regulate an AI-driven economy that may expand beyond the reach of traditional governance mechanisms. This study adopts a literature synthesis and comparative policy analysis approach to propose a six-pillar policy framework tailored for Vietnam. The framework aims to simultaneously foster AI development and mitigate associated risks in the digital age, thereby laying a strategic foundation for Vietnam to engage proactively, safely, and effectively with the Agent Economy.

items.title: Nonlinear Identification and Early Warning of Stablecoin Price Depegging: Empirical Evidence Based on a Cusp Catastrophe Model
items.abstract: Abstract Stablecoin prices stay close to $1 most of the time, but in a few periods they deviate markedly. Using daily data on four stablecoins (USDT, USDC, DAI, and FRAX) from 2019 to 2023, we introduce a cusp catastrophe model to identify the depegging process and compare two measures, price deviation and log return. We find the following. First, the jumps identified under the two measures differ substantially: jumps are sparse under the price deviation measure and frequent under the log return measure. Price deviation corresponds to the degree of departure from the peg, whereas log return corresponds to short-term price movements, so an assessment of stablecoin stability should distinguish these two dimensions. Second, differences in jump behavior depend on market embeddedness and the supply-and-demand adjustment mechanism. Traditional financial market variables are most broadly associated with price deviations of USDT and USDC. Although both are fiat-backed, the expansion of market capitalization works in opposite directions for USDT and USDC. For USDT it is associated with larger deviations because of issuance and distribution frictions, whereas for USDC it is associated with converging deviations through a direct redemption channel. Hence, the level of risk depends on liquidity characteristics and redemption arrangements. Third, on-chain capital flows and holdings concentration have forward-looking early-warning power for depegging; moderate deviations are best monitored over short horizons, and severe depegging is identified most effectively over a 7-day horizon. We provide empirical evidence from a nonlinear perspective for understanding the micro-level pricing mechanism of digital assets.

items.title: Get In, Decide, Prove: A Merchant-Side Readiness Benchmark for Agentic Commerce
items.abstract: AI agents now browse and buy on people's behalf, and benchmarks measure how well the agents perform. Far less is known about the other side of the transaction: whether a merchant's website lets an agent in, publishes terms precise enough to decide a purchase, and leaves evidence of what was agreed. This paper presents a merchant-side benchmark built on those three questions and reports a pilot of it. The central measurement, decision sufficiency, rates each criterion of a concrete buyer mandate (total cost, cancellation or return terms, service date, variant identity) as determinate, indeterminate, or unknown from the merchant's own published evidence. Readiness scores carry their evidence coverage and missingness bounds; access is reported separately for a declared bot, a declared headless browser, and a user-present browser; and each observed term is mapped to the RAILS admissibility class of the evidence that could support it in a dispute. Four large merchants received the full assessment: three refused the declared profiles at their offer pages, and no mandate could be confirmed as met, because each merchant left a total or a refund term undetermined. An access census of 555 sites of merchants that two payment processors publicly name as clients found the home page unreadable to both declared profiles at 105 sites (18.9%). A declared assessment of 330 merchants, scored by deterministic rules without a rater, found that evidence coverage rather than the score decides who can be ranked: 115 merchants (35%) reached the ranking threshold, rankable profiles scored a median of 89 to 90, and material terms was the one pillar well below the others, because the all-in total was decidable at 18 merchants. The pilot shows that the measurements can be taken; it does not validate them or rank merchants, and the weights and the projected clearing band await validation against outcomes.

items.title: Cryptomercantilism vs Monetary Sovereignty: How Stablecoin Laws Shape the Battle for International Monetary Supremacy
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Stablecoins are privately issued cryptocurrencies whose value is pegged to official currencies such as the US dollar. Their ease of use on the global level opens up a new front in global currency competition. This article asks how the EU and US—the issuers of the world’s two leading currencies—approach stablecoins through their respective legal frameworks. We contrast a US strategy of cryptomercantilism with an EU strategy of monetary sovereignty. These strategies yield legal frameworks that look similar on the surface but diverge sharply in substance. The US’s GENIUS Act aims to enhance the dollar’s dominance in global payment systems and stimulate new demand for US assets, particularly government bonds. The EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCAR) serves to safeguard the state’s ability to govern money. We conclude by discussing how the euro area and other countries can react to US cryptomercantilism, highlighting new challenges related to regulatory equivalence agreements and fungibility of tokens issued in different jurisdictions.
